In mathematics, '''Schubert polynomials''' are generalizations of [[Schur polynomials]] that represent cohomology classes of [[Schubert cycle]]s in [[Generalized flag variety|flag varieties]]. They were introduced by {{harvtxt|Lascoux|Schützenberger|1982}} and are named after [[Hermann Schubert]].

==Background==

{{harvtxt|Lascoux|1995}} described the history of Schubert polynomials.

The Schubert polynomials <math>\mathfrak{S}_w</math> are polynomials in the variables <math>x_1,x_2,\ldots</math> depending on an element <math>w</math> of the infinite symmetric group <math>S_\infty</math> of all permutations of <math>\N</math> fixing all but a finite number of elements. They form a basis for the polynomial ring <math>\Z[x_1,x_2,\ldots]</math> in infinitely many variables.

The cohomology of the flag manifold <math>\text{Fl}(m)</math> is <math>\Z[x_1, x_2,\ldots, x_m]/I,</math> where <math>I</math> is the ideal generated by homogeneous symmetric functions of positive degree. The Schubert polynomial <math>\mathfrak{S}_w</math> is the unique [[homogeneous polynomial]] of degree <math>\ell(w)</math> representing the Schubert cycle of <math> w</math> in the cohomology of the [[Generalized flag variety|flag manifold]] <math>\text{Fl}(m)</math> for all sufficiently large <math>m.</math>{{citation needed|date=February 2014}}

==Properties==

*If <math> w_0</math> is the permutation of longest length in <math>S_n</math> then <math>\mathfrak{S}_{w_0} = x_1^{n-1}x_2^{n-2} \cdots x_{n-1}^1</math>

* <math> \partial_i \mathfrak{S}_w = \mathfrak{S}_{ws_i}</math> if <math> w(i) > w(i+1)</math>, where <math>s_i</math> is the transposition <math>(i, i+1)</math> and where <math> \partial_i</math> is the divided difference operator taking <math>P</math> to <math>(P - s_iP)/(x_i - x_{i+1})</math>.

Schubert polynomials can be calculated recursively from these two properties. In particular, this implies that <math>\mathfrak{S}_w = \partial_{w^{-1}w_0} x_1^{n-1}x_2^{n-2} \cdots x_{n-1}^1</math>.

Other properties are

*<math>\mathfrak{S}_{id} = 1</math>

*If <math>s_i</math> is the transposition <math>(i,i+1)</math>, then <math>\mathfrak{S}_{s_i} = x_1 + \cdots + x_i </math>.

*If <math>w(i) < w(i + 1) </math> for all <math>i \neq r</math>, then <math>\mathfrak{S}_w</math> is the Schur polynomial <math>s_\lambda(x_1,\ldots,x_r)</math> where <math>\lambda</math> is the partition <math>(w(r) - r, \ldots, w(2) - 2, w(1) - 1)</math>. In particular all Schur polynomials (of a finite number of variables) are Schubert polynomials.

*Schubert polynomials have positive coefficients. A conjectural rule for their coefficients was put forth by [[Richard P. Stanley]], and proven in two papers, one by [[Sergey Fomin]] and Stanley and one by [[Sara Billey]], William Jockusch, and Stanley.

*The Schubert polynomials can be seen as a generating function over certain combinatorial objects called ''pipe dreams'' or ''rc-graphs''. These are in [[bijection]] with ''reduced Kogan faces'', (introduced in the PhD thesis of Mikhail Kogan) which are special faces of the Gelfand-Tsetlin polytope.

* Schubert polynomials also can be written as a weighted sum of objects called ''bumpless pipe dreams''. 

As an example 

:<math>\mathfrak{S}_{51423}(x) = x_1 x_3^2 x_4 x_2^2+x_1^2 x_3 x_4 x_2^2+x_1^2 x_3^2 x_4 x_2.</math>

==Multiplicative structure constants==

Since the Schubert polynomials form a <math>\mathbb Z</math>-basis, there are unique coefficients <math>c^{\alpha}_{\beta\gamma}</math> 
such that 

:<math>\mathfrak{S}_\beta \mathfrak{S}_\gamma = \sum_\alpha c^{\alpha}_{\beta\gamma} \mathfrak{S}_\alpha.</math>

These can be seen as a generalization of the Littlewood−Richardson coefficients described by the [[Littlewood–Richardson rule]].
For algebro-geometric reasons ([[Steven_Kleiman#Selected_publications|Kleiman's transversality theorem of 1974]]), these coefficients are non-negative integers and it is an 
outstanding problem in [[representation theory]] and [[combinatorics]] to give a combinatorial rule for these numbers.

==Double Schubert polynomials==

Double Schubert polynomials <math>\mathfrak{S}_w(x_1,x_2,\ldots, y_1,y_2,\ldots)</math> are polynomials in two infinite sets of variables, parameterized by an element ''w'' of the infinite [[symmetric group]], that becomes the usual Schubert polynomials when all the variables <math>y_i</math> are <math>0</math>.

The double Schubert polynomial <math>\mathfrak{S}_w(x_1,x_2,\ldots, y_1,y_2,\ldots)</math> are characterized by the properties

*<math>\mathfrak{S}_w(x_1,x_2,\ldots, y_1,y_2,\ldots) = \prod\limits_{i + j \leq n} (x_i - y_j)</math> when <math>w</math> is the permutation on <math>1,\ldots,n</math> of longest length.

*<math> \partial_i \mathfrak{S}_w = \mathfrak{S}_{ws_i}</math> if <math> w(i) > w(i+1).</math>

The double Schubert polynomials can also be defined as 

:<math>\mathfrak{S}_w(x,y) =\sum_{ w=v^{-1}u \text{ and } \ell(w)=\ell(u)+\ell(v) } \mathfrak{S}_u(x) \mathfrak{S}_v(-y).</math>

==Quantum Schubert polynomials==

{{harvtxt|Fomin|Gelfand|Postnikov|1997}} introduced quantum Schubert polynomials, that have the same relation to the [[Quantum cohomology#Small quantum cohomology|(small) quantum cohomology]] of flag manifolds that ordinary Schubert polynomials have to the ordinary cohomology.

==Universal Schubert polynomials==

{{harvtxt|Fulton|1999}} introduced universal Schubert polynomials, that generalize classical and quantum Schubert polynomials. He also described universal double Schubert polynomials generalizing double Schubert polynomials.
